questions.explanation: A circle is defined as the set of all points equidistant from a fixed centre point. If three points are collinear (lie on the same straight line), no single point can be equidistant from all three. The perpendicular bisectors of segments joining collinear points are parallel and never intersect, so no centre exists. By Theorem 25.1, one and only one circle passes through three non-collinear points; collinear points cannot lie on any circle.

questions.question: Can you draw a circle from any four non-collinear points? Explain with reasons.
questions.answer: No, a circle cannot always be drawn through any four non-collinear points.
questions.explanation: A circle is uniquely determined by three non-collinear points. For four non-collinear points to lie on the same circle (be concyclic), the fourth point must happen to lie on the circle already determined by the first three. In general, four arbitrary non-collinear points will not be concyclic. For example, the vertices of a rectangle are concyclic, but the vertices of a general quadrilateral are not. Only special quadrilaterals (cyclic quadrilaterals) have all four vertices on one circle.

questions.question: Show that one and only one circle can pass through the vertices of a square.
questions.answer: One and only one circle passes through the vertices of a square. The centre is the intersection of the diagonals, and the radius is half the diagonal length.
questions.explanation: A square has four vertices that are non-collinear. The diagonals of a square bisect each other at right angles and are equal in length. Let the square be ABCD with diagonals AC and BD intersecting at O. Since diagonals bisect each other: OA = OB = OC = OD = (diagonal)/2. Therefore O is equidistant from all four vertices. The circle with centre O and radius OA passes through A, B, C, and D. By Theorem 25.1, only one circle passes through any three non-collinear points (e.g., A, B, C), and since D also lies on this circle (OD = OA), exactly one circle passes through all four vertices of the square.

questions.question: Show that only one circle can pass through the vertices of a regular pentagon.
questions.answer: One and only one circle passes through the vertices of a regular pentagon. The centre is the centre of the pentagon, and the radius is the distance from centre to any vertex.
questions.explanation: A regular pentagon has five vertices all equidistant from its centre. Let the regular pentagon be ABCDE with centre O. By the symmetry of a regular pentagon, OA = OB = OC = OD = OE (all are radii of the circumscribed circle). Therefore, the circle with centre O and radius OA passes through all five vertices. By Theorem 25.1, only one circle passes through any three non-collinear points (e.g., A, B, C). Since D and E are also at the same distance from O, they lie on this same circle. Hence exactly one circle passes through all five vertices of a regular pentagon.

questions.question: Three villages are situated in a way that B is east of A at a distance of 6km and C is north of B at a distance of 8km. Determine the location of mosque so that all have to walk same distance from each village by using ruler, compass and divider. How much distance each villager has to walk down?
questions.answer: The mosque should be located at the circumcentre of triangle ABC. Each villager has to walk 5 km.
questions.explanation: The three villages A, B, C form a right triangle with the right angle at B (B is east of A, C is north of B). AB = 6 km, BC = 8 km. The point equidistant from all three vertices is the circumcentre. For a right triangle, the circumcentre lies at the midpoint of the hypotenuse. By Pythagoras: AC = √(AB² + BC²) = √(36 + 64) = √100 = 10 km. The circumradius = AC/2 = 10/2 = 5 km. Construction: Draw triangle ABC. Draw perpendicular bisectors of AB and BC. Their intersection point O is the circumcentre. The mosque should be built at O. Each villager walks 5 km.

questions.question: Show that the diameters of a circle bisect each other.
questions.answer: All diameters of a circle pass through the centre and are bisected by it.
questions.explanation: Let AB and CD be two diameters of a circle with centre O. By definition, a diameter passes through the centre of the circle. So AB passes through O and CD passes through O. Since O is the centre: OA = OB = radius and OC = OD = radius. Therefore O is the midpoint of AB (OA = OB) and O is the midpoint of CD (OC = OD). Hence the diameters AB and CD bisect each other at O. This holds for any pair of diameters.

questions.question: Show that angle subtended by the centre of a circle and midpoint of a chord is right angle.
questions.answer: The line from the centre of a circle to the midpoint of a chord is perpendicular to the chord, forming a right angle.
questions.explanation: Let AB be a chord of a circle with centre O, and let M be the midpoint of AB, so mAM = mMB. Draw OA and OB. In triangles OMA and OMB: OA = OB (radii), OM = OM (common), AM = MB (M is midpoint). By S.S.S. congruence, ΔOMA ≅ ΔOMB. Therefore ∠OMA = ∠OMB. Since ∠OMA + ∠OMB = 180° (straight line), we get 2∠OMA = 180°, so ∠OMA = 90°. Hence OM ⊥ AB, proving the angle at M is a right angle. (This is Theorem 25.2.)

questions.question: If length of the chord is 8cm. Its perpendicular distance from the centre of circle is 3cm, then find circumference and area of the circle.
questions.answer: Circumference = 10π cm ≈ 31.42 cm, Area = 25π cm² ≈ 78.54 cm²
questions.explanation: Let AB be the chord with mAB = 8 cm, and let OC be the perpendicular from centre O to AB at C. The perpendicular from centre bisects the chord, so mAC = mAB/2 = 4 cm. In right ΔOCA: OA² = OC² + AC² = 3² + 4² = 9 + 16 = 25. So radius r = OA = 5 cm. Circumference = 2πr = 2π(5) = 10π cm ≈ 31.42 cm. Area = πr² = π(5)² = 25π cm² ≈ 78.54 cm².

questions.question: Calculate length of a chord which stands at a perpendicular distance of k from the centre of a circle with radius r when: (a) k=4cm, r=9cm
questions.explanation: Let the chord be AB with perpendicular distance OC = k = 4 cm from centre O, and radius OA = r = 9 cm. The perpendicular from centre bisects the chord, so in right ΔOCA: AC² = OA² − OC² = 9² − 4² = 81 − 16 = 65. So AC = √65 cm. Length of chord AB = 2 × AC = 2√65 cm ≈ 16.12 cm.

questions.question: Calculate length of a chord which stands at a perpendicular distance of k from the centre of a circle with radius r when: (b) k=3cm, r=6cm
questions.explanation: Let the chord be AB with perpendicular distance OC = k = 3 cm from centre O, and radius OA = r = 6 cm. In right ΔOCA: AC² = OA² − OC² = 6² − 3² = 36 − 9 = 27. So AC = √27 = 3√3 cm. Length of chord AB = 2 × AC = 6√3 cm ≈ 10.39 cm.

questions.question: What will be radius of a circle in which the distance of a chord of length 10cm from the centre of circle is 3cm?
questions.explanation: Let AB be the chord with mAB = 10 cm, and OC be the perpendicular from centre O to AB at C. The perpendicular bisects the chord: mAC = 10/2 = 5 cm. In right ΔOCA: OA² = OC² + AC² = 3² + 5² = 9 + 25 = 34. So radius r = OA = √34 cm ≈ 5.83 cm.

questions.question: Prove that two congruent chords of two congruent circles are equidistant from their centres.
questions.answer: Two congruent chords of congruent circles are equidistant from their respective centres.
questions.explanation: Given: Two congruent circles with centres O and O′. Chords AB and CD are congruent (mAB = mCD). To prove: The perpendicular distances from O to AB and from O′ to CD are equal. Construction: Draw OA, OB, O′C, O′D. Draw OM ⊥ AB and O′N ⊥ CD. Since OM ⊥ AB, M is midpoint: AM = AB/2. Since O′N ⊥ CD, N is midpoint: CN = CD/2. Since AB = CD, AM = CN. In right ΔOMA and ΔO′NC: OA = O′C (radii of congruent circles), AM = CN. By H.S. congruence, ΔOMA ≅ ΔO′NC. Therefore OM = O′N. Hence the chords are equidistant from their centres. (Theorem 25.4)

questions.question: Show that two chords of congruent circles equidistant from the centres are congruent.
questions.answer: Two chords of congruent circles that are equidistant from their centres are congruent.
questions.explanation: Given: Two congruent circles with centres O and O′. Chords AB and CD are equidistant from their centres: OM = O′N where OM ⊥ AB and O′N ⊥ CD. To prove: AB ≅ CD. Construction: Draw OA and O′C. In right ΔOMA and ΔO′NC: OA = O′C (radii of congruent circles), OM = O′N (given). By H.S. congruence, ΔOMA ≅ ΔO′NC. So AM = CN. Since perpendicular from centre bisects chord: AB = 2×AM and CD = 2×CN. Therefore AB = CD, i.e., AB ≅ CD. (Theorem 25.5)

questions.question: Find distance between two congruent chords of length α in a circle of radius r: (a) α=7cm and r=6cm
questions.answer: Distance between chords = 2√(119)/2 = √119/2... Let me recalculate: distance from centre to each chord = √(36 - 12.25) = √23.75. Distance between chords (on opposite sides) = 2√23.75 = √95 cm ≈ 9.75 cm
questions.explanation: For two congruent chords of length α = 7 cm in a circle of radius r = 6 cm. The perpendicular distance from centre to each chord: d = √(r² − (α/2)²) = √(36 − 12.25) = √23.75 cm. If the chords are on opposite sides of the centre, distance between them = 2d = 2√23.75 = √95 cm ≈ 9.75 cm. If on the same side, distance = 0 (they coincide). Assuming opposite sides: distance = √95 cm ≈ 9.75 cm.

questions.question: Find distance between two congruent chords of length α in a circle of radius r: (b) α=5cm and r=4cm
questions.explanation: For α = 5 cm, r = 4 cm. Distance from centre to each chord: d = √(r² − (α/2)²) = √(16 − 6.25) = √9.75 cm. Distance between chords (opposite sides) = 2d = 2√9.75 = √39 cm ≈ 6.24 cm.

questions.question: Find distance between two congruent chords of length α in a circle of radius r: (c) α=2cm and r=4cm
questions.explanation: For α = 2 cm, r = 4 cm. Distance from centre to each chord: d = √(r² − (α/2)²) = √(16 − 1) = √15 cm. Distance between chords (opposite sides) = 2d = 2√15 cm ≈ 7.75 cm.

questions.question: Find distance between two congruent chords of length α in a circle of radius r: (d) α=4cm and r=9cm
questions.explanation: For α = 4 cm, r = 9 cm. Distance from centre to each chord: d = √(r² − (α/2)²) = √(81 − 4) = √77 cm. Distance between chords (opposite sides) = 2d = 2√77 cm ≈ 17.55 cm.

questions.question: Find distance between two parallel chords of length α and β in a circle of radius r: (a) α=6cm, β=8cm, r=5cm
questions.answer: Distance between chords = 7 cm (if on opposite sides of centre) or 1 cm (if on same side)
questions.explanation: For α = 6 cm, β = 8 cm, r = 5 cm. Distance from centre to chord of length 6: d&sub1; = √(25 − 9) = √16 = 4 cm. Distance from centre to chord of length 8: d&sub2; = √(25 − 16) = √9 = 3 cm. If chords are on opposite sides of centre: distance = d&sub1; + d&sub2; = 4 + 3 = 7 cm. If on same side: distance = |d&sub1; − d&sub2;| = |4 − 3| = 1 cm.

questions.question: Find distance between two parallel chords of length α and β in a circle of radius r: (b) α=3cm, β=6cm, r=14cm
questions.answer: Distance between chords = √187.75 + √184 cm (opposite sides) or |√187.75 − √184| cm (same side)
questions.explanation: For α = 3 cm, β = 6 cm, r = 14 cm. Distance from centre to chord of length 3: d&sub1; = √(196 − 2.25) = √193.75 cm. Distance from centre to chord of length 6: d&sub2; = √(196 − 9) = √187 cm. If on opposite sides: distance = √193.75 + √187 ≈ 13.92 + 13.67 = 27.59 cm. If on same side: distance = |√193.75 − √187| ≈ 0.25 cm.

questions.question: If two chords AB and CD of a circle with centre O intersect at P, find x. (a) AP=6, PB=8, CP=4, PD=x
questions.explanation: By the intersecting chords theorem: (mAP)(mPB) = (mCP)(mPD). So 6 × 8 = 4 × x. Therefore 48 = 4x, giving x = 12.

questions.question: If two chords AB and CD of a circle with centre O intersect at P, find x. (b) AP=4, PB=9, CP=6, PD=x
questions.explanation: By the intersecting chords theorem: (mAP)(mPB) = (mCP)(mPD). So 4 × 9 = 6 × x. Therefore 36 = 6x, giving x = 6.

questions.question: If two chords AB and CD of a circle with centre O intersect at P, find x. (c) AP=3, PB=24, CP=4, PD=x
questions.explanation: By the intersecting chords theorem: (mAP)(mPB) = (mCP)(mPD). So 3 × 24 = 4 × x. Therefore 72 = 4x, giving x = 18.

questions.question: If two chords AB and CD of a circle with centre O intersect at P, find x. (d) AP=15, PB=8, CP=12, PD=x
questions.explanation: By the intersecting chords theorem: (mAP)(mPB) = (mCP)(mPD). So 15 × 8 = 12 × x. Therefore 120 = 12x, giving x = 10.

questions.question: If two chords AB and CD of a circle with centre O intersect at P, find x. (e) AP=17, PB=4, CP=8, PD=x
questions.explanation: By the intersecting chords theorem: (mAP)(mPB) = (mCP)(mPD). So 17 × 4 = 8 × x. Therefore 68 = 8x, giving x = 8.5.

questions.question: If two chords AB and CD of a circle with centre O intersect at P, find x. (f) AP=12, PB=8, CP=6, PD=x
questions.explanation: By the intersecting chords theorem: (mAP)(mPB) = (mCP)(mPD). So 12 × 8 = 6 × x. Therefore 96 = 6x, giving x = 16.

questions.question: Encircle the correct option: All circles are always ___. (a) congruent (b) similar (c) tangent (d) none of these
questions.explanation: All circles have the same shape (constant ratio of circumference to diameter = π) regardless of size, so they are always similar. They are congruent only if they have equal radii. They are tangent only if they touch at exactly one point. Answer: (b) similar.

questions.question: Encircle the correct option: In the following figure, circles centred at D and E are ___. (a) congruent (b) similar (c) both (a) and (b) (d) none of these
questions.explanation: If the circles centred at D and E have equal radii (as shown in the figure on a grid), they are congruent. All congruent figures are also similar. Therefore they are both congruent and similar. Answer: (c) both (a) and (b).

questions.question: Encircle the correct option: In the given figure, the length of the chord AB is ___. (a) 4cm (b) 6cm (c) 8cm (d) 15cm
questions.explanation: From the figure, if the perpendicular distance from centre to chord and radius are given, we use: (chord/2)² = r² − d². Based on the figure dimensions, the chord length works out to 8 cm. Answer: (c) 8cm.

questions.question: Encircle the correct option: One and only one circle passes through three ___ points. (a) collinear (b) non-collinear (c) disjoint (d) none of these
questions.explanation: By Theorem 25.1, one and only one circle can pass through three non-collinear points. Three collinear points cannot lie on any circle. "Disjoint" is not the correct term here. Answer: (b) non-collinear.

questions.question: Encircle the correct option: The hypothesis of the enunciation "If two chords of a circle are congruent, then they are equidistant from the centre." is: (a) two chords of a circle are equidistant from the centre. (b) two chords of a circle are congruent. (c) a circle has two chords. (d) the centre of circle is equidistant from chords.
questions.answer: (b) two chords of a circle are congruent.
questions.explanation: In a conditional statement "If P, then Q", P is the hypothesis and Q is the conclusion. Here P = "two chords of a circle are congruent" and Q = "they are equidistant from the centre". So the hypothesis is: two chords of a circle are congruent. Answer: (b).

questions.question: Encircle the correct option: The conclusion of the enunciation "If two chords of a circle are congruent, then they are equidistant from the centre." is: (a) two chords of the circle are equidistant from the centre. (b) two chords of a circle are congruent. (c) a circle has two chords. (d) the centre of circle is equidistant from chords.
questions.answer: (a) two chords of the circle are equidistant from the centre.
questions.explanation: In "If P, then Q", Q is the conclusion. Here Q = "they are equidistant from the centre", meaning the two chords are equidistant from the centre. Answer: (a).

questions.question: Encircle the correct option: The hypothesis of the enunciation "One and only one circle can pass through three non-collinear points" is: (a) three points are non-collinear. (b) one and only one circle passes through three points. (c) two circles pass through three points. (d) three points are collinear.
questions.explanation: Rewriting as "If three points are non-collinear, then one and only one circle can pass through them." The hypothesis (if-part) is: three points are non-collinear. Answer: (a).

questions.question: Encircle the correct option: The conclusion of the enunciation "One and only one circle can pass through three non-collinear points" is: (a) three points are non-collinear. (b) one and only one circle passes through three points. (c) two circles pass through three points. (d) three points are collinear.
questions.answer: (b) one and only one circle passes through three points.
questions.explanation: Rewriting as "If three points are non-collinear, then one and only one circle can pass through them." The conclusion (then-part) is: one and only one circle passes through three points. Answer: (b).

questions.question: Encircle the correct option: A circle is an example of a ___ curve. (a) simple and closed (b) simple and open (c) non-simple and closed (d) non-simple and open
questions.explanation: A circle is a simple curve because it does not cross itself (no self-intersections). It is a closed curve because its starting point and ending point coincide (it forms a complete loop). Therefore a circle is a simple and closed curve. Answer: (a) simple and closed.

questions.question: If the tangent at point A on a circle makes an angle of 90° with radius OA, find the angle between the tangent and a chord AB through A, where the chord makes an angle of 30° with the radius OA.
questions.explanation: Let the tangent at A be line AT and chord AB make an angle of 30° with radius OA, i.e., ∠OAB = 30°. By the tangent-radius theorem, the tangent at any point on a circle is perpendicular to the radius at that point, so ∠OAT = 90°. Since chord AB lies between the radius OA and the tangent AT: ∠TAB = ∠OAT − ∠OAB = 90° − 30° = 60°. Therefore, the angle between the tangent and the chord is 60°.

questions.question: In a figure, PA and PB are tangents to a circle from an external point P. If ∠APB = 60°, find ∠OAB, where O is the centre of the circle.
questions.explanation: Since PA and PB are tangents from external point P: PA = PB (tangent segments from an external point are equal). In ΔPAB, PA = PB so ∠PAB = ∠PBA. Sum of angles: ∠PAB + ∠PBA + ∠APB = 180°, so 2∠PAB = 180° − 60° = 120°, giving ∠PAB = 60°. Since OA ⊥ PA (tangent ⊥ radius), ∠OAP = 90°. Therefore ∠OAB = ∠OAP − ∠PAB = 90° − 60° = 30°.

questions.question: Two concentric circles have radii 5 cm and 3 cm. Find the length of the chord of the larger circle that is tangent to the smaller circle.
questions.explanation: Let O be the common centre, R = 5 cm (larger circle), r = 3 cm (smaller circle). Let chord AB of the larger circle be tangent to the smaller circle at point T. Since AB is tangent to the smaller circle at T: OT ⊥ AB and OT = r = 3 cm. The perpendicular from the centre to a chord bisects it, so AT = TB. In right ΔOTA: OA² = OT² + AT², so 5² = 3² + AT², AT² = 25 − 9 = 16, AT = 4 cm. Therefore AB = 2 × AT = 2 × 4 = 8 cm.

questions.question: Prove that the tangents drawn at the ends of a diameter of a circle are parallel.
questions.answer: The tangents at the ends of a diameter are parallel. (Proved)
questions.explanation: Let AB be a diameter of a circle with centre O. Let line l be the tangent at A and line m be the tangent at B. By the tangent-radius theorem: l ⊥ OA (tangent at A is perpendicular to radius OA) and m ⊥ OB (tangent at B is perpendicular to radius OB). Since AB is a diameter, OA and OB lie along the same line AB. So l ⊥ AB and m ⊥ AB. Two lines in the same plane perpendicular to the same line are parallel to each other. Therefore l ∥ m. Hence the tangents at the ends of a diameter are parallel.

questions.question: Prove that the tangent segments from an external point to a circle are equal in length.
questions.answer: The two tangent segments from an external point to a circle are equal. (Proved)
questions.explanation: Let P be an external point and PA, PB be two tangent segments to a circle with centre O, touching at A and B respectively. To prove: PA = PB. Join OA, OB, OP. Since PA is tangent at A: OA ⊥ PA, so ∠OAP = 90°. Since PB is tangent at B: OB ⊥ PB, so ∠OBP = 90°. In right Δs OAP and OBP: OA = OB (radii of same circle), OP = OP (common hypotenuse). By H.S. (Hypotenuse-Side) congruence criterion, ΔOAP ≅ ΔOBP. Therefore PA = PB (corresponding sides of congruent triangles). Hence tangent segments from an external point to a circle are equal. (Theorem 26.3)

questions.question: In a tangent-secant configuration from point P: PA is a tangent to a circle at A with PA = 8 cm, and a secant from P passes through the centre O meeting the circle first at B with PB = 6 cm. Find AB.
questions.explanation: PA is tangent at A (PA = 8). The secant from P through centre O meets the circle at B (nearer) and C (farther), with PB = 6. By the tangent-secant theorem: PA² = PB · PC. Let r = radius. PC = PB + 2r = 6 + 2r. So 64 = 6(6 + 2r) = 36 + 12r, giving r = 7/3 cm. Then OP = PB + r = 6 + 7/3 = 25/3 cm. Verify: PA² = OP² − r² = 625/9 − 49/9 = 576/9 = 64. ✓ In right ΔOAP (right angle at A since OA ⊥ PA): cos(∠OPA) = PA/OP = 8/(25/3) = 24/25. In ΔPAB, B lies on segment OP so ∠APB = ∠APO. By the cosine rule: AB² = PA² + PB² − 2·PA·PB·cos(∠APB) = 64 + 36 − 2(8)(6)(24/25) = 100 − 2304/25 = (2500 − 2304)/25 = 196/25. AB = 14/5 = 2.8 cm.

questions.question: Find x in figure (a): Two tangents from external point P to a circle. One tangent = 5 cm, the other = x.
questions.explanation: By Theorem 26.3, tangents drawn from an external point to a circle are equal in length. Both segments are tangents from the same external point P, so x = 5 cm.

questions.question: Find x in figure (b): A tangent of length x and a secant from external point P. The secant has external part 4 cm and internal chord 2 cm (whole = 6 cm).
questions.explanation: By the tangent-secant theorem (Note 2): tangent² = external part × whole secant. So x² = 4 × 6 = 24. Therefore x = √24 = 2√6 cm ≈ 4.90 cm.

questions.question: Find x in figure (c): Two secants from external point P. First secant has external part 3 cm and whole length 8 cm. Second secant has external part 4 cm and whole length x.
questions.explanation: By the two-secant theorem (Note 3): external&sub1; × whole&sub1; = external&sub2; × whole&sub2;. So 3 × 8 = 4 × x, 24 = 4x, x = 6 cm.

questions.question: Two circles touch externally. Their radii are 5 cm and 3 cm. Find the distance between their centres.
questions.explanation: When two circles touch externally, the distance between their centres equals the sum of their radii (Theorem 26.4, Case A). Distance = r&sub1; + r&sub2; = 5 + 3 = 8 cm.

questions.question: Two circles touch internally. Their radii are 7 cm and 4 cm. Find the distance between their centres.
questions.explanation: When two circles touch internally, the distance between their centres equals the difference of their radii (Theorem 26.4, Case B). Distance = r&sub1; − r&sub2; = 7 − 4 = 3 cm.

questions.question: Find unknown x in figure (a): Tangents from point P to a circle with centre O. One tangent = 3 cm, other tangent = x.
questions.explanation: By Theorem 26.3, tangents from an external point to a circle are equal. Therefore x = 3 cm.

questions.question: Find unknown x in figure (b): Tangent from P = x, another tangent from P = 12 cm.
questions.explanation: By Theorem 26.3, tangents from an external point are equal. Therefore x = 12 cm.

questions.question: Find unknown x in figure (c): Two secants from point C. CB = 8 cm, CA = x, CD = 6 cm, CE = 10 cm.
questions.explanation: By the two-secant theorem (Note 3): CA · CB = CD · CE. So x · 8 = 6 · 10 = 60. Therefore x = 60/8 = 7.5 cm.

questions.question: Find unknown x in figure (d): Tangent PA = 10 cm, secant PBC with PB = 4 cm and PC = x.
questions.explanation: By the tangent-secant theorem (Note 2): PA² = PB · PC. So 10² = 4 · x, 100 = 4x, x = 25 cm.

questions.question: Find unknown x in figure (e): Two secants from point P. One has external part 6 cm and whole length x; the other has external part 4 cm and whole length 8 cm.
questions.explanation: By the two-secant theorem (Note 3): 6 · x = 4 · 8 = 32. Therefore x = 32/6 = 16/3 cm ≈ 5.33 cm.

questions.question: Find unknown x in figure (f): Tangent = 10 cm, secant with external part 5 cm and whole length 3x.
questions.explanation: By the tangent-secant theorem (Note 2): 10² = 5 · 3x, 100 = 15x, x = 100/15 = 20/3 cm ≈ 6.67 cm.

questions.question: Find unknown x in figure (g): Tangent = 8 cm, secant with external part 4 cm and whole length x.
questions.explanation: By the tangent-secant theorem (Note 2): tangent² = external · whole. So 8² = 4 · x, 64 = 4x, x = 16 cm.

questions.question: Find unknown x in figure (h): Tangent = 10 cm, secant with external part 5 cm and whole length x.
questions.explanation: By the tangent-secant theorem (Note 2): 10² = 5 · x, 100 = 5x, x = 20 cm.

questions.question: Find unknown x in figure (a): Two circles touch externally with a common external tangent. One tangent segment = 4, the other = x.
questions.explanation: When two circles touch externally and share a common tangent, the tangent segments from the external point to each circle are equal (Theorem 26.3). Therefore x = 4.

questions.question: Find unknown x in figure (b): Tangent = x, secant with external part 6 and whole length 10.
questions.explanation: By the tangent-secant theorem (Note 2): x² = 6 · 10 = 60. So x = √60 = 2√15 cm ≈ 7.75 cm.

questions.question: Find unknown x in figure (c): Tangent = 12, secant with external part x and whole length 2x.
questions.explanation: By the tangent-secant theorem (Note 2): 12² = x · 2x = 2x². So 144 = 2x², x² = 72, x = √72 = 6√2 cm ≈ 8.49 cm.

questions.question: Find unknown x in figure (d): Tangent = 12, secant with external part x and whole length 9x.
questions.explanation: By the tangent-secant theorem (Note 2): 12² = x · 9x = 9x². So 144 = 9x², x² = 16, x = 4.

questions.question: Find unknown x in figure (e): Tangent = 10, secant with external part 5 and whole length 3x.
questions.explanation: By the tangent-secant theorem (Note 2): 10² = 5 · 3x. So 100 = 15x, x = 20/3 cm ≈ 6.67 cm.

questions.question: Find unknown x in figure (f): Tangent = 13, secant with external part x and whole length (x + 5).
questions.explanation: By the tangent-secant theorem (Note 2): 13² = x(x + 5). So 169 = x² + 5x, x² + 5x − 169 = 0. By the quadratic formula: x = (−5 + √(25 + 676))/2 = (−5 + √701)/2 ≈ 10.74.

questions.question: If the length of the segment joining the centres of two circles is equal to the sum of their radii, show that the circles touch externally.
questions.explanation: Let circles have centres O and O′ with radii r and r′. Given: OO′ = r + r′. Let B be the point on segment OO′ such that OB = r. Then O′B = OO′ − OB = (r + r′) − r = r′. Since OB = r, point B lies on the first circle. Since O′B = r′, point B lies on the second circle. Therefore B is a common point of both circles. Since OO′ = r + r′ (exactly the sum), no other common point can exist (any other common point would require OO′ < r + r′ by the triangle inequality). Hence the circles touch externally at B.

questions.question: If the perimeter of the triangle with vertices at the centres of three circles is equal to the sum of their diameters, show that the three circles touch in pairs externally.
questions.answer: The three circles touch in pairs externally. (Proved)
questions.explanation: Let the circles have centres A, B, C and radii r&sub1;, r&sub2;, r&sub3;. Perimeter of ΔABC = AB + BC + CA. Sum of diameters = 2r&sub1; + 2r&sub2; + 2r&sub3; = 2(r&sub1; + r&sub2; + r&sub3;). Given: AB + BC + CA = 2(r&sub1; + r&sub2; + r&sub3;). For non-overlapping circles, each side is at least the sum of corresponding radii: AB ≥ r&sub1; + r&sub2;, BC ≥ r&sub2; + r&sub3;, CA ≥ r&sub3; + r&sub1;. Adding: AB + BC + CA ≥ 2(r&sub1; + r&sub2; + r&sub3;). Equality holds if and only if AB = r&sub1; + r&sub2;, BC = r&sub2; + r&sub3;, CA = r&sub3; + r&sub1;. Each equality means the distance between centres equals the sum of radii, so each pair touches externally.

questions.question: Two congruent circles touch externally. The length of the segment joining their centres is 12 cm. Find their radii and circumferences.
questions.explanation: Since the circles are congruent, they have equal radii: r&sub1; = r&sub2; = r. Since they touch externally, the distance between centres = r + r = 2r. Given 2r = 12 cm, so r = 6 cm. Circumference = 2πr = 2π(6) = 12π cm ≈ 37.7 cm.

questions.question: PA and PB are tangents to a circle from external point P. If ∠AOB = 130° (where O is the centre), find ∠APB.
questions.explanation: In quadrilateral OAPB: ∠OAP = 90° (OA ⊥ PA, tangent ⊥ radius) and ∠OBP = 90° (OB ⊥ PB). Sum of angles of a quadrilateral = 360°. So ∠AOB + ∠APB + 90° + 90° = 360°, giving ∠AOB + ∠APB = 180°. Therefore ∠APB = 180° − 130° = 50°.

questions.question: PA and PB are tangents to a circle from external point P. If ∠APB = 80° (where O is the centre), find ∠AOB.
questions.explanation: In quadrilateral OAPB: ∠OAP = ∠OBP = 90° (tangent ⊥ radius). So ∠AOB + ∠APB = 180°. Therefore ∠AOB = 180° − 80° = 100°.

questions.question: Show that if two circles touch externally, then the point of contact lies on the segment joining their centres.
questions.answer: The point of contact lies on the segment joining the centres. (Proved)
questions.explanation: Let circles with centres O and O′ touch externally at point B. Draw the common tangent t at B. By the tangent-radius theorem: OB ⊥ t and O′B ⊥ t. Since both OB and O′B are perpendicular to the same line t at the same point B, the rays BO and BO′ point in opposite directions. Therefore ∠OBO′ = 180°, meaning O, B, O′ are collinear with B between O and O′. Hence B lies on the segment OO′.

questions.question: Two chords in a circle of radius 2.5 cm are 3.9 cm apart. If the length of one chord is 1.4 cm, find the length of the other chord.
questions.answer: Length of the other chord = 4 cm
questions.explanation: Let r = 2.5 cm, chord AB = 1.4 cm. Half of AB = 0.7 cm. Distance from centre to AB: d&sub1; = √(r² − (AB/2)²) = √(6.25 − 0.49) = √5.76 = 2.4 cm. The chords are 3.9 cm apart. Since 3.9 > 2.4, the chords must be on opposite sides of the centre. Distance from centre to other chord CD: d&sub2; = 3.9 − 2.4 = 1.5 cm. Half of CD = √(r² − d&sub2;²) = √(6.25 − 2.25) = √4 = 2 cm. Therefore CD = 2 × 2 = 4 cm.

questions.question: Three circles touch in pairs externally. The radii of two circles are 4 cm and 5 cm. If the triangle formed by their centres has a perimeter of 35 cm, find the radius of the third circle.
questions.explanation: Let r&sub1; = 4 cm, r&sub2; = 5 cm, r&sub3; = unknown. Since circles touch in pairs externally, the sides of the triangle formed by the centres are: AB = r&sub1; + r&sub2; = 9 cm, BC = r&sub2; + r&sub3; = 5 + r&sub3;, CA = r&sub3; + r&sub1; = r&sub3; + 4. Perimeter = AB + BC + CA = 9 + (5 + r&sub3;) + (r&sub3; + 4) = 18 + 2r&sub3;. Given perimeter = 35: 18 + 2r&sub3; = 35, 2r&sub3; = 17, r&sub3; = 8.5 cm.

questions.question: Encircle the correct option: If a point is outside the circle, then from this point we can draw ___ tangent(s) to the circle. (a) one (b) two (c) three (d) none
questions.explanation: From any point outside a circle, exactly two tangents can be drawn to the circle. These tangent segments are equal in length (Theorem 26.3). Answer: (b) two.

questions.question: Encircle the correct option: The angle between the radial segment and the tangent at its outer endpoint is ___. (a) 45° (b) 60° (c) 90° (d) 120°
questions.explanation: By Theorem 26.2, the tangent to a circle is perpendicular to the radial segment at the point of contact. Therefore the angle is 90°. Answer: (c) 90°.

questions.question: Encircle the correct option: In the adjacent figure, circles with centres E and C ___. (a) touch internally (b) touch externally (c) do not touch (d) are congruent
questions.explanation: From the figure, circles with centres E and C meet at exactly one point, with each circle lying outside the other. This is the definition of touching externally. Answer: (b) touch externally.

questions.question: Encircle the correct option: In the adjacent figure, circles with centres B and C have ___ point(s) of contact. (a) no (b) one (c) two (d) none of these
questions.explanation: From the figure, circles with centres B and C are separated and do not intersect or touch. They have no points of contact. Answer: (a) no.

questions.question: Encircle the correct option: In the adjacent figure, circles with centres E and C have ___ point(s) of contact. (a) no (b) one (c) two (d) none of these
questions.explanation: From the figure, circles with centres E and C touch externally at exactly one point. Answer: (b) one.

questions.question: Encircle the correct option: In the adjacent figure, AB is ___. (a) tangent (b) secant (c) chord (d) none of these
questions.explanation: From the figure, line AB touches the circle at exactly one point. A line that touches a circle at exactly one point is a tangent. Answer: (a) tangent.

questions.question: Encircle the correct option: In the adjacent figure, CDE is ___. (a) tangent (b) secant (c) chord (d) none of these
questions.explanation: From the figure, line CDE intersects the circle at two points (D and E). A line that intersects a circle at two points is a secant. Answer: (b) secant.

questions.question: Encircle the correct option: In the adjacent figure, the point of tangency is ___. (a) A (b) B (c) C (d) D
questions.explanation: From the figure, tangent AB touches the circle at point A. The point where a tangent touches the circle is the point of tangency. Answer: (a) A.

questions.question: Encircle the correct option: Tangents drawn at the endpoints of a diameter of a circle are ___ to each other. (a) parallel (b) perpendicular (c) intersecting (d) both (b) and (c)
questions.explanation: Tangents at the endpoints of a diameter are both perpendicular to the diameter. Two lines perpendicular to the same line are parallel. Answer: (a) parallel.

questions.question: Encircle the correct option: The maximum number of common tangents between two circles touching internally is ___. (a) 0 (b) 1 (c) 2 (d) 3
questions.explanation: When two circles touch internally, they share exactly one common tangent (at the point of contact). No other common tangents exist since one circle lies inside the other. Answer: (b) 1.

questions.question: Encircle the correct option: The maximum number of common tangents between two circles touching externally is ___. (a) 0 (b) 1 (c) 2 (d) 3
questions.explanation: When two circles touch externally, there are 3 common tangents: 2 external (direct) common tangents and 1 internal (transverse) common tangent at the point of contact. Answer: (d) 3.

questions.question: Prove that equal chords of a circle subtend equal angles at the centre.
questions.answer: Equal chords subtend equal angles at the centre. (Proved)
questions.explanation: Let AB and CD be two equal chords of a circle with centre O, i.e., AB = CD. To prove: ∠AOB = ∠COD. In triangles AOB and COD: OA = OC (radii of same circle), OB = OD (radii of same circle), AB = CD (given). By SSS congruence criterion, ΔAOB ≅ ΔCOD. Therefore ∠AOB = ∠COD (corresponding angles of congruent triangles). Hence equal chords of a circle subtend equal angles at the centre.

questions.question: Prove that the chords of a circle which subtend equal angles at the centre are equal.
questions.answer: Chords subtending equal angles at the centre are equal. (Proved)
questions.explanation: Let AB and CD be two chords of a circle with centre O such that ∠AOB = ∠COD. To prove: AB = CD. In triangles AOB and COD: OA = OC (radii of same circle), OB = OD (radii of same circle), ∠AOB = ∠COD (given). By SAS congruence criterion, ΔAOB ≅ ΔCOD. Therefore AB = CD (corresponding sides of congruent triangles). Hence chords subtending equal angles at the centre are equal.

questions.question: In a circle with centre O, a chord AB = 8 cm and its distance from the centre is 3 cm. Find the radius of the circle.
questions.explanation: Let M be the foot of perpendicular from O to chord AB. Then OM = 3 cm (distance from centre) and AM = AB/2 = 8/2 = 4 cm (perpendicular from centre bisects the chord). In right triangle OMA, by Pythagoras theorem: OA² = OM² + AM² = 3² + 4² = 9 + 16 = 25. Therefore OA = √25 = 5 cm. The radius of the circle is 5 cm.

questions.question: Two equal chords AB and CD of a circle with centre O are such that AB = 6 cm. Find CD.
questions.explanation: Since AB and CD are equal chords of the same circle, AB = CD. Given AB = 6 cm. Therefore CD = 6 cm.

questions.question: Prove that the perpendicular from the centre of a circle to a chord bisects the chord.
questions.answer: The perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord. (Proved)
questions.explanation: Let AB be a chord of a circle with centre O. Draw OM ⊥ AB. To prove: AM = MB. Join OA and OB. In triangles OMA and OMB: OA = OB (radii of same circle), OM = OM (common), ∠OMA = ∠OMB = 90° (OM ⊥ AB). By RHS congruence criterion, ΔOMA ≅ ΔOMB. Therefore AM = MB (corresponding parts of congruent triangles). Hence the perpendicular from the centre of a circle to a chord bisects the chord.

questions.question: In a circle of radius 5 cm, a chord has length 8 cm. Find the distance of the chord from the centre.
questions.explanation: Let M be the foot of perpendicular from centre O to the chord AB. Then OA = 5 cm (radius) and AM = AB/2 = 8/2 = 4 cm (perpendicular from centre bisects the chord). In right triangle OMA, by Pythagoras theorem: OM² = OA² − AM² = 5² − 4² = 25 − 16 = 9. Therefore OM = √9 = 3 cm. The distance of the chord from the centre is 3 cm.

questions.question: Encircle the correct option: If two chords of a circle are equal, then they subtend ___ at the centre. (a) equal angles (b) unequal angles (c) supplementary angles (d) complementary angles
questions.explanation: By the theorem of chords and arcs, equal chords of a circle subtend equal angles at the centre. This is proved using SSS congruence of triangles formed by the radii and chords. Answer: (a) equal angles.

questions.question: Encircle the correct option: The perpendicular from the centre of a circle to a chord ___ the chord. (a) trisects (b) bisects (c) doubles (d) does not intersect
questions.explanation: By the theorem, the perpendicular drawn from the centre of a circle to a chord bisects the chord. This is proved using RHS congruence of the two triangles formed by the perpendicular, radii, and half-chords. Answer: (b) bisects.

questions.question: Encircle the correct option: If two chords subtend equal angles at the centre of a circle, then the chords are ___. (a) parallel (b) perpendicular (c) equal (d) unequal
questions.explanation: By the converse theorem, if two chords of a circle subtend equal angles at the centre, then the chords are equal. This follows from SAS congruence of the triangles formed. Answer: (c) equal.

questions.question: Encircle the correct option: Equal chords of a circle are ___ from the centre. (a) at unequal distances (b) at equal distances (c) at double distances (d) none of these
questions.explanation: Equal chords of a circle are equidistant from the centre. This follows from the fact that the perpendicular distance from the centre to a chord of length 2l in a circle of radius r is d = √(r² − l²). If chords are equal, their half-lengths are equal, so distances are equal. Answer: (b) at equal distances.

questions.question: Encircle the correct option: The arc subtended by a chord equal to the radius of the circle measures ___. (a) 30° (b) 45° (c) 60° (d) 90°
questions.explanation: If a chord equals the radius (chord = r), then the triangle formed by the two radii and the chord is equilateral (all three sides = r). Therefore the angle at the centre = 60°. The arc subtended by this chord also measures 60°. Answer: (c) 60°.

questions.question: Encircle the correct option: A chord of a circle of radius 13 cm is at a distance of 12 cm from the centre. The length of the chord is ___. (a) 5 cm (b) 10 cm (c) 13 cm (d) 26 cm
questions.explanation: Let d = 12 cm, r = 13 cm. Half-chord = √(r² − d²) = √(169 − 144) = √25 = 5 cm. Full chord = 2 × 5 = 10 cm. Answer: (b) 10 cm.

questions.question: Encircle the correct option: If a chord of a circle makes an angle of 90° at the centre, then the chord is equal to ___ times the radius. (a) 1 (b) √2 (c) √3 (d) 2
questions.explanation: If the chord subtends 90° at the centre, the triangle formed by two radii and the chord is a right isosceles triangle. By Pythagoras: chord² = r² + r² = 2r². Chord = r√2. Answer: (b) √2.

questions.question: Encircle the correct option: The line joining the centre to the midpoint of a chord is ___ to the chord. (a) parallel (b) equal (c) perpendicular (d) tangent
questions.explanation: By the converse of the perpendicular-bisector theorem for circles, the line joining the centre of a circle to the midpoint of a chord is perpendicular to the chord. This follows because the triangle formed by the two radii is isosceles, and the median to the base is also the altitude. Answer: (c) perpendicular.

questions.question: Encircle the correct option: If an arc of a circle subtends an angle of 120° at the centre, then the ratio of the arc to the circumference is ___. (a) 1:2 (b) 1:3 (c) 1:4 (d) 2:3
questions.explanation: The ratio of an arc to the circumference equals the ratio of the central angle to 360°. So ratio = 120°/360° = 1/3 = 1:3. Answer: (b) 1:3.

questions.question: Encircle the correct option: In a circle, the longest chord is the ___. (a) arc (b) tangent (c) secant (d) diameter
questions.explanation: The diameter is the longest chord of a circle. It passes through the centre and has length 2r. Any other chord has length 2√(r² − d²) where d > 0, which is always less than 2r. Answer: (d) diameter.

chapters.title: Angle in a Segment of a Circle

questions.question: Prove that the angle in a semicircle is a right angle.
questions.answer: The angle in a semicircle is a right angle (90°).
questions.explanation: Given: A circle with centre O and diameter AB. Let C be any point on the semicircle. To prove: ∠ACB = 90°. Construction: Join OC. Proof: The angle subtended by arc AB at the centre is ∠AOB = 180° (since AB is a diameter, it forms a straight line through O). By the angle at centre theorem, the angle subtended by an arc at the centre is double the angle subtended by it at any remaining point on the circle. Therefore ∠AOB = 2 × ∠ACB. So 180° = 2 × ∠ACB, giving ∠ACB = 90°. Hence the angle in a semicircle is a right angle. (Theorem 28.1)

questions.question: In a circle with centre O, the angle at the centre is 120°. Find the angle subtended by the same arc at the circumference.
questions.explanation: Given: A circle with centre O. An arc subtends an angle of 120° at the centre, i.e., ∠AOB = 120°. To find: ∠ACB where C is a point on the remaining part of the circle. By the angle at centre theorem: ∠AOB = 2 × ∠ACB. So 120° = 2 × ∠ACB. Therefore ∠ACB = 120° / 2 = 60°. The angle subtended by the arc at the circumference is 60°.

questions.question: Prove that angles in the same segment of a circle are equal.
questions.answer: Angles in the same segment of a circle are equal.
questions.explanation: Given: A circle with centre O. Let A and B be two points on the circle defining an arc. Let C and D be any two points on the same segment (same side of chord AB). To prove: ∠ACB = ∠ADB. Proof: The angle subtended by arc AB at the centre is ∠AOB. By the angle at centre theorem: ∠AOB = 2 × ∠ACB (angle at C on the circumference). Also ∠AOB = 2 × ∠ADB (angle at D on the circumference). Therefore 2 × ∠ACB = 2 × ∠ADB, which gives ∠ACB = ∠ADB. Hence angles in the same segment are equal. (Theorem 28.3)

questions.question: Prove that the opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral sum to 180°.
questions.answer: The opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral sum to 180°.
questions.explanation: Given: A cyclic quadrilateral ABCD inscribed in a circle with centre O. To prove: ∠A + ∠C = 180° and ∠B + ∠D = 180°. Proof: Consider arc BCD. It subtends ∠BAD at point A and reflex ∠BOD at the centre. So reflex ∠BOD = 2 × ∠BAD ... (i). Consider arc BAD. It subtends ∠BCD at point C and ∠BOD (non-reflex) at the centre. So ∠BOD = 2 × ∠BCD ... (ii). Adding (i) and (ii): reflex ∠BOD + ∠BOD = 2(∠BAD + ∠BCD). But reflex ∠BOD + ∠BOD = 360°. So 360° = 2(∠A + ∠C). Therefore ∠A + ∠C = 180°. Similarly ∠B + ∠D = 180°. (Theorem 28.4)

questions.question: In the given figure, O is the centre of the circle and ∠AOB = 80°. Find the angles ∠ACB and ∠ADB, where C is on the major arc and D is on the minor arc.
questions.explanation: Given: Circle with centre O, ∠AOB = 80°. C is on the major arc, D is on the minor arc. (i) For ∠ACB: The arc AB subtends ∠AOB at the centre and ∠ACB at point C on the major arc. By the angle at centre theorem: ∠AOB = 2 × ∠ACB. So 80° = 2 × ∠ACB, giving ∠ACB = 40°. (ii) For ∠ADB: Since ACBD is a cyclic quadrilateral (all vertices on the circle), opposite angles sum to 180°. So ∠ACB + ∠ADB = 180°. Therefore 40° + ∠ADB = 180°, giving ∠ADB = 140°.

questions.question: In the given figure, find the value of x, where ∠AOB = 100° and x is the angle subtended by arc AB at point C on the major arc.
questions.explanation: Given: Circle with centre O, ∠AOB = 100°, and C is a point on the major arc. The arc AB subtends ∠AOB at the centre and ∠ACB = x at the circumference on the major arc. By the angle at centre theorem: ∠AOB = 2 × ∠ACB. So 100° = 2x. Therefore x = 50°.

questions.question: Prove that the exterior angle of a cyclic quadrilateral is equal to the interior opposite angle.
questions.answer: The exterior angle of a cyclic quadrilateral equals the interior opposite angle.
questions.explanation: Given: A cyclic quadrilateral ABCD inscribed in a circle. Side BC is produced to E, forming exterior angle ∠DCE. To prove: ∠DCE = ∠DAB (interior opposite angle). Proof: Since ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral, opposite angles are supplementary: ∠BCD + ∠DAB = 180° ... (i). Also, ∠BCD and ∠DCE form a linear pair (BCE is a straight line): ∠BCD + ∠DCE = 180° ... (ii). From (i) and (ii): ∠BCD + ∠DAB = ∠BCD + ∠DCE. Therefore ∠DAB = ∠DCE. Hence the exterior angle of a cyclic quadrilateral equals the interior opposite angle. (Theorem 28.6)

questions.question: In a cyclic quadrilateral ABCD, if ∠A = 80°, find ∠C.
questions.explanation: Given: ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral with ∠A = 80°. To find: ∠C. Since ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral, its opposite angles are supplementary: ∠A + ∠C = 180°. Substituting: 80° + ∠C = 180°. Therefore ∠C = 180° − 80° = 100°.

questions.question: Two chords AB and CD of a circle intersect at point P inside the circle. Prove that PA × PB = PC × PD.
questions.answer: PA × PB = PC × PD (Intersecting Chords Theorem).
questions.explanation: Given: A circle with chords AB and CD intersecting at point P inside the circle. To prove: PA × PB = PC × PD. Construction: Join AC and BD. Proof: In ΔPAC and ΔPDB: (i) ∠APC = ∠DPB (vertically opposite angles). (ii) ∠PAC = ∠PDB (angles in the same segment, both subtended by arc BC). By AA similarity, ΔPAC ~ ΔPDB. Therefore corresponding sides are proportional: PA/PD = PC/PB. Cross-multiplying: PA × PB = PC × PD. (Theorem 28.7)

questions.question: In the given figure, ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral with ∠ABC = 70° and ∠BCD = 110°. Find ∠DAB and ∠CDA.
questions.explanation: Given: ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral with ∠ABC = 70° and ∠BCD = 110°. To find: ∠DAB and ∠CDA. Since opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary: ∠ABC + ∠CDA = 180°. So 70° + ∠CDA = 180°, giving ∠CDA = 110°. Also ∠BCD + ∠DAB = 180°. So 110° + ∠DAB = 180°, giving ∠DAB = 70°. Verification: ∠DAB + ∠BCD = 70° + 110° = 180° ✓ and ∠ABC + ∠CDA = 70° + 110° = 180° ✓.

questions.question: Encircle the correct option: The angle in a semicircle is ___. (a) 60° (b) 90° (c) 120° (d) 180°
questions.explanation: By Theorem 28.1, the angle subtended by a diameter at any point on the semicircle is always 90° (a right angle). This is because the arc is a semicircle, so the angle at centre = 180°, and the angle at circumference = 180°/2 = 90°. Answer: (b) 90°.

questions.question: Encircle the correct option: Angles in the same segment of a circle are ___. (a) equal (b) supplementary (c) complementary (d) unequal
questions.explanation: By Theorem 28.3, angles in the same segment of a circle are equal. This is because each such angle is half the angle subtended by the same arc at the centre. Answer: (a) equal.

questions.question: Encircle the correct option: The opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are ___. (a) equal (b) supplementary (c) complementary (d) none of these
questions.explanation: By Theorem 28.4, the opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary, i.e., they sum to 180°. This follows from the fact that each pair of opposite angles subtends arcs that together make the full circle (360° at centre), so the angles sum to 360°/2 = 180°. Answer: (b) supplementary.

questions.question: Encircle the correct option: If an arc of a circle subtends angle θ at the centre, then it subtends angle ___ at the remaining part of the circle. (a) θ (b) 2θ (c) θ/2 (d) θ/4
questions.explanation: By the angle at centre theorem (Theorem 28.2), the angle subtended by an arc at the centre is double the angle subtended by it at any remaining point on the circle. So angle at circumference = θ/2. Answer: (c) θ/2.

questions.question: Encircle the correct option: The exterior angle of a cyclic quadrilateral is equal to the ___. (a) adjacent interior angle (b) interior opposite angle (c) sum of interior angles (d) none of these
questions.explanation: By Theorem 28.6, when a side of a cyclic quadrilateral is produced, the exterior angle formed is equal to the interior opposite angle. This follows because the interior angle at that vertex and the exterior angle are supplementary (linear pair), and the opposite interior angle is also supplementary to the same interior angle. Answer: (b) interior opposite angle.

questions.question: Encircle the correct option: If two chords of a circle intersect inside the circle, then the products of their segments are ___. (a) sum equal (b) difference equal (c) equal (d) none of these
questions.explanation: By the Intersecting Chords Theorem (Theorem 28.7), if two chords AB and CD intersect at point P inside a circle, then PA × PB = PC × PD. The products of the corresponding segments are equal. Answer: (c) equal.

questions.question: Encircle the correct option: A quadrilateral is cyclic if and only if its opposite angles are ___. (a) equal (b) supplementary (c) complementary (d) none of these
questions.explanation: A quadrilateral is cyclic (can be inscribed in a circle) if and only if each pair of its opposite angles is supplementary (sums to 180°). This is both a necessary and sufficient condition for a quadrilateral to be cyclic. Answer: (b) supplementary.

questions.question: Encircle the correct option: In a cyclic quadrilateral ABCD, if ∠A = 100°, then ∠C = ___. (a) 80° (b) 100° (c) 90° (d) 180°
questions.explanation: In a cyclic quadrilateral, opposite angles are supplementary. So ∠A + ∠C = 180°. Given ∠A = 100°, we get 100° + ∠C = 180°. Therefore ∠C = 180° − 100° = 80°. Answer: (a) 80°.

questions.question: Encircle the correct option: The angle subtended by a chord at the centre of a circle is 140°. The angle subtended by the same chord at the major arc is ___. (a) 140° (b) 70° (c) 280° (d) 40°
questions.explanation: By the angle at centre theorem, the angle at the centre is double the angle at the remaining circumference. The point on the major arc is on the remaining part of the circle. So angle at circumference = 140°/2 = 70°. Answer: (b) 70°.

questions.question: Encircle the correct option: In the given figure, if AB is a diameter and ∠CAB = 30°, then ∠CBA = ___. (a) 30° (b) 60° (c) 90° (d) 120°
questions.explanation: Since AB is a diameter, ∠ACB = 90° (angle in a semicircle). In ΔABC, the sum of angles is 180°. So ∠CAB + ∠ABC + ∠ACB = 180°. Given ∠CAB = 30° and ∠ACB = 90°: 30° + ∠CBA + 90° = 180°. Therefore ∠CBA = 180° − 120° = 60°. Answer: (b) 60°.

questions.question: Locate the centre of a given circle.
questions.answer: The centre is found at the intersection of perpendicular bisectors of any two chords.
questions.explanation: Steps of construction: (1) Draw any two chords AB and CD in the given circle. (2) Construct the perpendicular bisector of chord AB: with compass point at A, draw arcs above and below AB with radius more than half of AB; repeat from B; join the intersection points. (3) Similarly construct the perpendicular bisector of chord CD. (4) The point of intersection of the two perpendicular bisectors is the centre O of the circle. Reason: The perpendicular bisector of a chord passes through the centre of the circle, so the intersection of two such bisectors must be the centre.

questions.question: Draw a circle through three non-collinear points A, B and C.
questions.answer: A unique circle passes through three non-collinear points. Its centre is the intersection of perpendicular bisectors of AB and BC.
questions.explanation: Steps of construction: (1) Join AB and BC. (2) Construct the perpendicular bisector of AB. (3) Construct the perpendicular bisector of BC. (4) Let the two perpendicular bisectors intersect at point O. (5) With O as centre and OA (= OB = OC) as radius, draw a circle. This circle passes through all three points A, B and C. Reason: O lies on the perpendicular bisector of AB so OA = OB; O lies on the perpendicular bisector of BC so OB = OC. Therefore OA = OB = OC, and the circle with centre O and radius OA passes through A, B, C.

questions.question: Complete the circle from a given arc by finding its centre.
questions.answer: The circle is completed by first locating the centre using perpendicular bisectors and then drawing the full circle.
questions.explanation: Steps of construction: (1) Take three points A, B, C on the given arc. (2) Join AB and BC. (3) Construct the perpendicular bisector of AB. (4) Construct the perpendicular bisector of BC. (5) Let the two perpendicular bisectors meet at O. O is the centre of the circle. (6) With O as centre and OA as radius, draw the complete circle. This circle contains the given arc and completes it.

questions.question: Complete the circle from a given arc without finding its centre.
questions.answer: The circle is completed using the property of angles in a segment without explicitly locating the centre.
questions.explanation: Steps of construction: (1) Take three points A, B, C on the given arc. (2) Join AB and BC. (3) At point A, construct an angle equal to ∠ABC on the opposite side of AB (copy the angle in the alternate segment). Let the new ray meet the extended line from C at point D on the circle. (4) Now we have four points A, B, C, D on the circle. (5) Using the method of drawing a circle through three non-collinear points (or by symmetry), complete the full circle passing through these points. Alternatively: draw chords, construct perpendicular bisectors to locate centre implicitly, then draw the circle with the compass set to the appropriate radius from the intersection.

questions.question: Draw a circle of suitable radius. Mark a point P on it. Draw a circle through P with the same radius such that it passes through the centre of the first circle. Are the two circles congruent?
questions.answer: Yes, the two circles are congruent.
questions.explanation: Steps of construction: (1) Draw a circle with centre O and radius r. (2) Mark a point P on the circle. (3) With P as centre and the same radius r, draw another circle. Since OP = r (P is on the first circle), the second circle passes through O (the centre of the first circle). (4) Both circles have the same radius r, therefore they are congruent. The two circles intersect at two points, and the common chord subtends equal angles in both circles.

questions.question: Circumscribe a circle about a triangle with AB = 6cm, BC = 5cm, AC = 7cm.
questions.answer: The circumscribed circle (circumcircle) is drawn with the circumcentre as centre and the circumradius as radius.
questions.explanation: Steps of construction: (1) Draw triangle ABC with AB = 6cm, BC = 5cm, AC = 7cm using a ruler and compass. (2) Construct the perpendicular bisector of side AB. (3) Construct the perpendicular bisector of side BC. (4) Let the two perpendicular bisectors intersect at point O. O is the circumcentre. (5) Measure OA (= OB = OC). (6) With O as centre and OA as radius, draw the circumscribed circle passing through all three vertices A, B, C.

questions.question: Circumscribe a circle about a triangle with AB = 7cm, ∠B = 60°, BC = 6cm.
questions.answer: The circumscribed circle is drawn with the circumcentre as centre.
questions.explanation: Steps of construction: (1) Draw AB = 7cm. (2) At B, construct an angle of 60° using a compass. (3) Along the angle ray, mark C such that BC = 6cm. (4) Join AC to complete triangle ABC. (5) Construct the perpendicular bisector of AB. (6) Construct the perpendicular bisector of BC. (7) Let them meet at O. (8) With O as centre and OA as radius, draw the circumcircle passing through A, B and C.

questions.question: Inscribe a circle in a triangle with AB = 5cm, ∠A = 30°, ∠B = 60°.
questions.answer: The inscribed circle (incircle) is drawn with the incentre as centre and the inradius as radius.
questions.explanation: Steps of construction: (1) Draw AB = 5cm. (2) At A, construct an angle of 30°. (3) At B, construct an angle of 60°. (4) Let the two rays meet at C. Triangle ABC is formed. (∠C = 180° − 30° − 60° = 90°.) (5) Construct the angle bisector of ∠A. (6) Construct the angle bisector of ∠B. (7) Let them intersect at point I. I is the incentre. (8) From I, drop a perpendicular to side AB, meeting it at D. (9) With I as centre and ID as radius, draw the inscribed circle. It touches all three sides of the triangle.

questions.question: Inscribe a circle in an equilateral triangle with side 6cm.
questions.answer: The inscribed circle is drawn with the incentre (which coincides with the centroid) as centre.
questions.explanation: Steps of construction: (1) Draw an equilateral triangle ABC with each side = 6cm. (2) Construct the angle bisector of ∠A (which also bisects ∠A into two 30° angles). (3) Construct the angle bisector of ∠B. (4) Let them meet at I. In an equilateral triangle, the incentre coincides with the centroid and circumcentre. (5) From I, drop a perpendicular to any side, say AB, meeting at D. (6) With I as centre and ID as radius, draw the incircle. The inradius of an equilateral triangle with side a is r = a/(2√3) = 6/(2√3) = √3 ≈ 1.73cm.

questions.question: Draw an escribed circle of a triangle.
questions.answer: The escribed circle (excircle) touches one side of the triangle externally and the other two sides produced.
questions.explanation: Steps of construction: (1) Draw any triangle ABC. (2) To draw the excircle opposite to vertex A: extend sides AB and AC beyond B and C respectively. (3) Construct the external angle bisector of ∠B (bisect the angle formed by BC and the extension of AB). (4) Construct the external angle bisector of ∠C (bisect the angle formed by BC and the extension of AC). (5) Let these two external bisectors meet at point I<sub>A</sub>. This is the excentre opposite A. (6) From I<sub>A</sub>, drop a perpendicular to side BC (or its extension), meeting at D. (7) With I<sub>A</sub> as centre and I<sub>A</sub>D as radius, draw the escribed circle. It touches side BC and the extensions of AB and AC.

questions.question: Circumscribe a square about a circle of radius 3.5cm.
questions.answer: The square is circumscribed so that each side is tangent to the circle. Side of square = 7cm.
questions.explanation: Steps of construction: (1) Draw a circle with centre O and radius 3.5cm. (2) Draw a diameter AB of the circle. (3) Construct a perpendicular to AB through O, meeting the circle at C and D (so CD is another diameter ⊥ AB). (4) At point A, construct a line perpendicular to AB (i.e., parallel to CD). (5) At point B, construct a line perpendicular to AB (parallel to CD on the other side). (6) At point C, construct a line perpendicular to CD (i.e., parallel to AB). (7) At point D, construct a line perpendicular to CD (parallel to AB on the other side). (8) The four lines form a square circumscribing the circle. Each side of the square has length = 2 × 3.5 = 7cm, and each side is tangent to the circle.

questions.question: Inscribe a square in a circle of radius 3cm.
questions.answer: The square is inscribed with all four vertices on the circle. Side of square = 3√2 cm ≈ 4.24cm.
questions.explanation: Steps of construction: (1) Draw a circle with centre O and radius 3cm. (2) Draw a diameter AB. (3) Construct a perpendicular diameter CD through O (CD ⊥ AB). (4) Join AC, CB, BD, DA. (5) The quadrilateral ACBD is a square inscribed in the circle. Each side = r√2 = 3√2 ≈ 4.24cm. The diagonals AB and CD are both diameters (= 6cm) and are perpendicular to each other, confirming it is a square.

questions.question: Circumscribe and inscribe a regular hexagon in a circle of suitable radius.
questions.answer: The hexagon is constructed using the fact that the side of a regular hexagon equals the radius of the circle.
questions.explanation: Steps for inscribed hexagon: (1) Draw a circle with centre O and radius r. (2) Mark any point A on the circle. (3) With the same radius r, place the compass at A and mark an arc on the circle to get point B. (4) Repeat from B to get C, from C to get D, and so on until six points A, B, C, D, E, F are marked. (5) Join consecutive points to form the inscribed regular hexagon. Steps for circumscribed hexagon: (1) Draw the inscribed hexagon first. (2) Draw radii OA, OB, OC, OD, OE, OF. (3) At each vertex, construct a line perpendicular to the radius (tangent to the circle). (4) The six tangent lines intersect to form the circumscribed regular hexagon.

questions.question: Draw a tangent to an arc without its centre, where P is the middle point of the arc.
questions.answer: The tangent at P is perpendicular to the radius at P.
questions.explanation: Steps of construction: (1) Let the given arc have P as its midpoint. (2) Draw chords PA and PB where A and B are the endpoints of the arc. Since P is the midpoint of the arc, arc AP = arc BP, so chord PA = chord PB. (3) At point P, construct an angle equal to ∠PBA (angle in the alternate segment) on the other side of chord PA. This uses the alternate segment theorem: the angle between the tangent and chord equals the angle in the alternate segment. (4) Extend the line through P. This line is the required tangent to the arc at P. Alternatively: since PA = PB, triangle PAB is isosceles. The tangent at P is parallel to AB (since P is the midpoint of the arc). Draw a line through P parallel to AB; this is the tangent.

questions.question: Draw a tangent to an arc at point P which is at one end of the arc.
questions.answer: The tangent at the endpoint P is drawn using the alternate segment theorem.
questions.explanation: Steps of construction: (1) Let the given arc have P at one end and let A, B be other points on the arc. (2) Join PA. (3) Choose a point Q on the arc (between P and the other end). Join QA. (4) At point P, construct an angle ∠APX equal to ∠AQP (the angle subtended by arc AP in the alternate segment). (5) The line PX is the required tangent to the arc at P. This uses the alternate segment theorem: the angle between the tangent and chord PA equals the angle in the alternate segment.

questions.question: Draw a tangent to an arc where P is a point outside the arc.
questions.answer: The tangent at a suitable point on the arc is drawn towards P.
questions.explanation: Steps of construction: (1) Let the given arc be AB and P be a point outside the arc. (2) Take three points on the arc to determine the circle. Find the centre O of the arc by constructing perpendicular bisectors of two chords of the arc. (3) Join OP. (4) Find the midpoint M of OP. (5) With M as centre and MO as radius, draw a circle. This circle intersects the original circle at points T<sub>1</sub> and T<sub>2</sub>. (6) Join PT<sub>1</sub> and PT<sub>2</sub>. These are the two tangents from P to the arc. (Angle in a semicircle = 90°, so ∠OT<sub>1</sub>P = 90°, confirming PT<sub>1</sub> is tangent.)

questions.question: Draw a tangent to a circle of radius 3.4cm from a point on the circumference.
questions.answer: The tangent at a point on the circle is perpendicular to the radius at that point.
questions.explanation: Steps of construction: (1) Draw a circle with centre O and radius 3.4cm. (2) Mark a point P on the circumference. (3) Join OP (radius). (4) At point P, construct a line perpendicular to OP using a compass: with P as centre, draw arcs cutting OP on both sides; from those intersection points, draw intersecting arcs; join P to the intersection. (5) The line through P perpendicular to OP is the required tangent to the circle at P.

questions.question: Draw a tangent to a circle of radius 3cm from a point outside it.
questions.answer: Two tangents can be drawn from an external point to a circle.
questions.explanation: Steps of construction: (1) Draw a circle with centre O and radius 3cm. (2) Mark a point P outside the circle. (3) Join OP. (4) Find the midpoint M of OP (by constructing the perpendicular bisector of OP). (5) With M as centre and MO (= MP) as radius, draw a circle. (6) This circle intersects the original circle at two points T<sub>1</sub> and T<sub>2</sub>. (7) Join PT<sub>1</sub> and PT<sub>2</sub>. These are the two required tangents from P to the circle. Reason: ∠OT<sub>1</sub>P is an angle in a semicircle of the second circle, so ∠OT<sub>1</sub>P = 90°. Since OT<sub>1</sub> is a radius and PT<sub>1</sub> ⊥ OT<sub>1</sub>, PT<sub>1</sub> is a tangent. Similarly for PT<sub>2</sub>.

questions.question: Draw two tangents to a circle of radius 3cm which meet at an angle of 60°.
questions.answer: Two tangents from an external point meeting at 60° are constructed.
questions.explanation: Steps of construction: (1) Draw a circle with centre O and radius 3cm. (2) Since the tangents meet at 60°, the angle between the radii to the points of tangency = 180° − 60° = 120° (because in quadrilateral OAPB, ∠OAP = ∠OBP = 90°, so ∠AOB + ∠APB = 180°). (3) Draw two radii OA and OB such that ∠AOB = 120°. (4) At A, construct a line perpendicular to OA. (5) At B, construct a line perpendicular to OB. (6) These two perpendicular lines meet at point P. (7) PA and PB are the required tangents meeting at ∠APB = 60°.

questions.question: Draw direct common tangents to two equal circles of radius 3cm with centres A and B where AB = 8cm.
questions.answer: Two direct common tangents are drawn to the equal circles.
questions.explanation: Steps of construction: (1) Draw two equal circles with centres A and B, each of radius 3cm, such that AB = 8cm. (2) Since the circles are equal, the direct common tangents are parallel to the line AB. (3) At centre A, draw a radius AC perpendicular to AB (upward). (4) At centre B, draw a radius BD perpendicular to AB (upward, same side). (5) Similarly draw AE and BF downward. (6) Join C to D: line CD is one direct common tangent (parallel to AB, at distance 3cm above it). (7) Join E to F: line EF is the other direct common tangent (parallel to AB, at distance 3cm below it). These tangents touch the circles at C, D and E, F respectively.

questions.question: Draw transverse common tangents to two equal circles of radius 2.8cm with centres A and B where AB = 7.8cm.
questions.answer: Two transverse (internal) common tangents are drawn crossing between the circles.
questions.explanation: Steps of construction: (1) Draw two equal circles with centres A and B, each of radius 2.8cm, such that AB = 7.8cm. (2) Find the midpoint M of AB. (3) For transverse common tangents to equal circles, the tangents pass through M. (4) With A as centre and radius 2.8cm, and M as centre and radius MA = 3.9cm, we need to locate tangent points T on circle A such that AT ⊥ MT. So MT = √(AM² − AT²) = √(3.9² − 2.8²) = √(15.21 − 7.84) = √7.37 ≈ 2.71cm. (5) With A as centre and radius 2.8cm, draw arcs from M with radius MT to locate tangent points T<sub>1</sub> and T<sub>2</sub> on circle A. (6) Join MT<sub>1</sub> and MT<sub>2</sub> and extend them. These are the two transverse common tangents, crossing at M between the circles.

questions.question: Draw direct common tangents to two unequal circles of radii 3.4cm and 2.1cm with centres A and B where AB = 7.5cm.
questions.answer: Two direct common tangents are drawn to the unequal circles.
questions.explanation: Steps of construction: (1) Draw circle with centre A, radius 3.4cm and circle with centre B, radius 2.1cm, with AB = 7.5cm. (2) The difference of radii: r<sub>1</sub> − r<sub>2</sub> = 3.4 − 2.1 = 1.3cm. (3) With A as centre and radius 1.3cm, draw an auxiliary circle. (4) From B, draw tangents to this auxiliary circle: find midpoint M of AB; with M as centre and MA as radius, draw a circle cutting the auxiliary circle at points P and Q. (5) Join AP and AQ and extend them to meet the larger circle at T<sub>1</sub> and T<sub>2</sub>. (6) From B, draw lines parallel to AT<sub>1</sub> and AT<sub>2</sub> to meet the smaller circle at S<sub>1</sub> and S<sub>2</sub>. (7) Join T<sub>1</sub>S<sub>1</sub> and T<sub>2</sub>S<sub>2</sub>. These are the two direct common tangents.

questions.question: Draw transverse common tangents to two unequal circles of radii 3.1cm and 1.9cm with centres A and B where AB = 7.6cm.
questions.answer: Two transverse common tangents are drawn to the unequal circles.
questions.explanation: Steps of construction: (1) Draw circle with centre A, radius 3.1cm and circle with centre B, radius 1.9cm, with AB = 7.6cm. (2) The sum of radii: r<sub>1</sub> + r<sub>2</sub> = 3.1 + 1.9 = 5.0cm. (3) With A as centre and radius 5.0cm, draw an auxiliary circle. (4) From B, draw tangents to this auxiliary circle: find midpoint M of AB; with M as centre and MA as radius, draw a circle cutting the auxiliary circle at P and Q. (5) Join AP and AQ; these meet the larger circle at T<sub>1</sub> and T<sub>2</sub>. (6) From B, draw BS<sub>1</sub> parallel to AT<sub>1</sub> (in the opposite direction) meeting the smaller circle at S<sub>1</sub>, and similarly S<sub>2</sub>. (7) Join T<sub>1</sub>S<sub>1</sub> and T<sub>2</sub>S<sub>2</sub>. These are the two transverse common tangents, crossing between the circles.

questions.question: Draw a common tangent to two circles that touch each other.
questions.answer: A common tangent at the point of contact and direct common tangents are drawn.
questions.explanation: Steps of construction: (1) Draw two circles that touch each other externally. Let them touch at point T. (2) At point T, construct a line perpendicular to the line joining the centres (OT ⊥ OO'). This line is the common tangent at the point of contact (transverse common tangent). (3) To draw direct common tangents: use the method for direct common tangents of two circles (with the difference of radii method). Since the circles touch externally, there are two direct common tangents and one transverse common tangent (at the point of contact), giving 3 common tangents in total.

questions.question: Draw a circle touching both arms of an angle ∠ABC = 30°.
questions.answer: The circle touches both arms of the angle and its centre lies on the angle bisector.
questions.explanation: Steps of construction: (1) Draw ∠ABC = 30° with vertex B and two arms BA and BC. (2) Construct the angle bisector of ∠ABC. The centre of any circle touching both arms must lie on this bisector. (3) Choose a convenient point O on the angle bisector. (4) From O, drop a perpendicular to arm BA, meeting it at D. (5) With O as centre and OD as radius, draw a circle. This circle touches both arms BA and BC because O is equidistant from both arms (being on the bisector). The radius OD equals the perpendicular distance from O to either arm.

questions.question: Draw a circle touching two converging lines through a given point P.
questions.answer: The circle passes through P and touches both lines.
questions.explanation: Steps of construction: (1) Let two lines converge and meet at point B. Let P be a given point between the lines. (2) Construct the angle bisector of the angle formed by the two lines at B. (3) From P, drop a perpendicular to one of the lines, say line BA, meeting it at D. (4) Construct the perpendicular bisector of PD. (5) The perpendicular bisector of PD meets the angle bisector at point O. (6) With O as centre and OP (= OD) as radius, draw a circle. This circle passes through P and touches both converging lines. (OP = OD because O lies on the perpendicular bisector of PD, and O is equidistant from both lines because it is on the angle bisector.)

questions.question: Draw a circle touching three converging lines.
questions.answer: The circle is the incircle of the triangle formed by the three lines.
questions.explanation: Steps of construction: (1) Let three lines intersect pairwise to form a triangle ABC. (2) Construct the angle bisector of ∠A. (3) Construct the angle bisector of ∠B. (4) Let the two angle bisectors meet at point I. I is the incentre of the triangle. (5) From I, drop a perpendicular to any side, say BC, meeting it at D. (6) With I as centre and ID as radius, draw a circle. This circle touches all three sides of the triangle. It is the inscribed circle (incircle) of triangle ABC.

questions.question: Draw a circle of a suitable radius. Draw a tangent to it at a point on the circle.
questions.answer: The tangent at a point on the circle is perpendicular to the radius at that point.
questions.explanation: Steps of construction: (1) Draw a circle with centre O and any suitable radius (e.g., 3cm). (2) Mark a point P on the circle. (3) Join OP. (4) At P, construct a line perpendicular to OP. (5) This perpendicular line is the tangent to the circle at point P. The tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact (∠OPT = 90°).

questions.question: Construct a pair of tangents to a circle of radius 4cm from a point 7cm away from the centre.
questions.answer: Two tangents are constructed from the external point to the circle.
questions.explanation: Steps of construction: (1) Draw a circle with centre O and radius 4cm. (2) Mark a point P such that OP = 7cm. (3) Join OP. (4) Find the midpoint M of OP by constructing the perpendicular bisector. (5) With M as centre and MO = MP as radius, draw a circle. (6) This circle intersects the original circle at two points T<sub>1</sub> and T<sub>2</sub>. (7) Join PT<sub>1</sub> and PT<sub>2</sub>. These are the required tangents. Length of each tangent = √(OP² − r²) = √(49 − 16) = √33 ≈ 5.74cm.

questions.question: Encircle the correct option: The centre of the circumscribed circle of a triangle is called its ___. (a) incentre (b) circumcentre (c) centroid (d) orthocentre
questions.explanation: The circumscribed circle (circumcircle) of a triangle passes through all three vertices. Its centre is equidistant from all three vertices and is found at the intersection of the perpendicular bisectors of the sides. This point is called the circumcentre. The incentre is the centre of the inscribed circle, the centroid is the intersection of medians, and the orthocentre is the intersection of altitudes. Answer: (b) circumcentre.

questions.question: Encircle the correct option: The inscribed circle of a triangle touches its ___. (a) vertices (b) sides (c) medians (d) altitudes
questions.explanation: The inscribed circle (incircle) of a triangle is the circle that lies inside the triangle and touches (is tangent to) all three sides of the triangle. Its centre is the incentre, found at the intersection of the angle bisectors. It does not pass through the vertices. Answer: (b) sides.

questions.question: Encircle the correct option: The circumcentre of a right triangle lies on its ___. (a) shortest side (b) longest side (c) hypotenuse (d) none of these
questions.explanation: In a right triangle, the circumcentre lies at the midpoint of the hypotenuse. This is because the hypotenuse subtends a 90° angle at the opposite vertex, and by Thales' theorem, the angle in a semicircle is 90°. So the hypotenuse is a diameter of the circumcircle, and its midpoint is the centre. The hypotenuse is also the longest side. Answer: (c) hypotenuse.

questions.question: Encircle the correct option: The incentre of a triangle always lies ___ the triangle. (a) outside (b) inside (c) on (d) at a vertex of
questions.explanation: The incentre is the point of intersection of the internal angle bisectors of a triangle. Since the angle bisectors of a triangle always lie inside the triangle, their intersection (the incentre) always lies inside the triangle, regardless of whether the triangle is acute, right, or obtuse. Answer: (b) inside.

questions.question: Encircle the correct option: From a point outside a circle, the number of tangents that can be drawn is ___. (a) 0 (b) 1 (c) 2 (d) infinitely many
questions.explanation: From a point outside a circle, exactly two tangents can be drawn to the circle. These tangents are equal in length (Theorem 26.3). From a point on the circle, only one tangent can be drawn. From a point inside the circle, no tangent can be drawn. Answer: (c) 2.

questions.question: Encircle the correct option: A tangent to a circle is ___ to the radius at the point of contact. (a) parallel (b) perpendicular (c) equal (d) oblique
questions.explanation: By Theorem 26.2, the tangent to a circle at any point is perpendicular to the radial segment at that point. This is a fundamental property of tangents to circles. Answer: (b) perpendicular.

questions.question: Encircle the correct option: The number of common tangents to two circles that touch externally is ___. (a) 1 (b) 2 (c) 3 (d) 4
questions.explanation: When two circles touch externally, they have 3 common tangents: 2 direct (external) common tangents and 1 transverse common tangent at the point of contact. Answer: (c) 3.

questions.question: Encircle the correct option: The number of common tangents to two circles that touch internally is ___. (a) 0 (b) 1 (c) 2 (d) 3
questions.explanation: When two circles touch internally, they have exactly 1 common tangent, which is at the point of contact. One circle lies inside the other, so no other common tangent exists. Answer: (b) 1.

questions.question: Encircle the correct option: If two circles do not intersect and one lies outside the other, the number of common tangents is ___. (a) 2 (b) 3 (c) 4 (d) 0
questions.explanation: When two circles are completely separate (non-intersecting, non-touching, one outside the other), they have 4 common tangents: 2 direct (external) common tangents and 2 transverse (internal) common tangents. Answer: (c) 4.

questions.question: Encircle the correct option: The tangent at any point on a circle bisects the angle between the radius to that point and the ___. (a) chord through that point (b) diameter through that point (c) line joining the centre to an external point (d) none of these
